summary: Talbott 2013 (23924268): randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 60 moderately stressed adults (56 completed); Relora 250 mg twice daily for 4 weeks lowered salivary cortisol by 18% and improved overall stress and POMS mood scores versus placebo. No primary outcome was designated, outcomes were unadjusted and authors had commercial ties, so credit is narrow (stress/mood only); weight and stress-eating outcomes were not measured. Per the fourth ruling set, credit is limited and outcome-specific, with the hierarchy uncertainty kept.

applicability.studied_population: Adults with moderate self-reported psychological stress taking Relora 500 mg/day for 4 weeks.

identity.standardization: Patented blend of Magnolia officinalis bark and Phellodendron amurense bark extracts, not less than 1.5% honokiol and 0.1% berberine

population.description: 60 adults screened for moderate psychological stress randomized (30 per arm); 56 completed (35 men, 21 women).

study_contexts.study_design: Randomized double-blind placebo-controlled parallel trial, 4 weeks; rice-flour placebo capsules; no designated primary outcome.

outcomes.name: Salivary cortisol exposure 18% lower than placebo at week 4 (p<0.05)
Overall Stress (Yale Stress Survey) -11% and POMS Global Mood State 11% better vs placebo (p<0.05); tension, depression, anger, fatigue, confusion lower and vigor higher

limitations: No primary outcome designated (multiple outcomes, unadjusted); recorded not_reported. Small 4-week trial.
Authors include employees of SupplementWatch and of MonaVie, which markets a supplement containing Relora (competing-interests statement).
Exact Relora combination only; no transfer to isolated magnolia, honokiol, phellodendron or berberine. Body-weight or stress-eating outcomes were not reported in this paper.
Returned decision A019: date-restricted hold; publication-age-only exclusion withdrawn.

Dr. Pham's fourth ruling set (2026-10-28): limited, outcome-specific stress credit for the exact Relora formula; outcome hierarchy uncertain (no primary designated; 56 completers; 4 weeks; full text read in PMC3750820). Cortisol and perceived-stress changes are not long-term health or disease prevention.
Context authored and source-verified by agent review (Claude) on 2026-10-28; Dr. Pham's pre-approval of fully source-verified contexts attested by Sean on 2026-10-28.

dose.administration_frequency: One 250 mg capsule with breakfast and one with dinner.
co_therapies: No assigned co-therapy; no concurrent-medication policy reported.
dose.reported_regimen: Relora 250 mg capsule twice daily (500 mg/day) for 4 weeks.

normalization.basis: 2 x 250 mg = 500 mg/day Relora as assigned.

source_provenance.location: Methods (supplement standardization; randomization and dosing; 60 screened/randomized, 56 completed; POMS and stress measures); Results Figures 1-3; competing interests

freshness_search.query: (Relora OR ("Magnolia officinalis" AND "Phellodendron") OR (magnolia AND phellodendron)) AND (stress OR anxiety OR cortisol OR mood) AND (meta-analysis[pt] OR systematic review[pt] OR randomized controlled trial[pt])

freshness_search.screening_rule: Exact Relora (Magnolia officinalis + Phellodendron amurense) human trials of any date, because the filtered search returned only two records. One record is a chick model and was excluded.

read.title: Effect of a proprietary Magnolia and Phellodendron extract on stress levels in healthy women: a pilot, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial.
read.finding: 2008 RCT, which predates the credited 2013 source: 40 overweight premenopausal women, Relora 250 mg three times daily for 6 weeks (26 completed). State anxiety (Spielberger STATE) improved vs placebo. Trait anxiety, salivary cortisol and amylase, appetite and sleep did not change.

freshness_search.conclusion: confirms: no Relora synthesis or RCT is newer than the credited 2013 trial (23924268). The older exact-preparation trial 18426577 found a state-anxiety benefit but no change in cortisol. That supports keeping the credit limited (stress/mood) with the outcome-hierarchy uncertainty recorded.
